verdict: Read alone, the introduction's key sentences give the story, the problem, and the tool, but the last one (k4) announces a topic, so the outline has no thesis until k17 in Part III. k5 through k12 tell a history without saying why it matters to software. From k13 on, the outline tells the argument well.

flags.quote: This Article explores how the discovery rule applies to software defects and what courts should make of the manufacturer's power to change the product after the sale.
flags.issue: The introduction's last key sentence announces a topic; the claim first appears at k17.

flags.quote: Moreover, the early exceptions were narrow.
flags.issue: Opens with a transition; the paragraph's point isn't tied to the argument.

flags.quote: In Hollis v. Brandt Manufacturing Co., the Twelfth Circuit applied the modern rule to a defective furnace valve that leaked for years before anyone noticed.
flags.issue: Opens with a case rather than a point, and sits out of order between the nineteenth-century rule and the mid-century disease cases.
Says what comes next in the history, not why it matters for software.
